title: Solaria Data - VPC lift-and-shift sizing & Terraform playbook (draft)
content:
Context and goal:

This is a working playbook for Solaria Data's requested lift-and-shift of Redwood Private into their on-prem VPC (primary region: solaria-dc-1). The goal is a production-ready minimum viable cluster that supports low-latency inference for internal analytics workloads (batch and real-time), integrates with customer KMS for key management, and leaves a clear upgrade path to Dedicated-style autoscaling in a later phase.

This draft is intentionally prescriptive — we want a clear, repeatable plan Solaria's infra team can follow and that our PS/SEs can execute alongside them.

High-level constraints from discovery call (customer-provided):
- Data center uses VMware ESXi 7.0 for compute host management; bare-metal options permitted for inference nodes if rack space available.
- On-prem network uses overlapping RFC1918 ranges with partner offices; Solaria will provide a NAT bridge and BGP peering to avoid IP conflicts.
- Private KMS (Vault HSM) available in solaria-dc-1, with network-restricted access only from designated subnets.
- Backups must be encrypted at rest and transit, and retained 90 days for logs and 365 days for model artifacts.
- Throughput requirement: baseline 200 qps for small text-generation models (Llama2-13B equivalent), with burst tolerance to 800 qps across workloads. 99th pctl latency target: <250ms for interactive paths.

Assumptions used for sizing (callout):
- We assume Redwood's runtime performance numbers for the target model family: 35–55 tokens/s per 80GB A100 GPU depending on batch size and quantization.
- Inference traffic distribution: 70% short-chats (avg 40 tokens), 30% long-batch (avg 600 tokens).
- N+2 redundancy required for controller tier and N+1 for serving tier for maintenance windows.
- Storage I/O dominated by model load and checkpoint writes: prefer NVMe for model cache, NFS for artifacts.

Recommended topology (phase 1 — baseline MV cluster):
- Network: dedicated VPC segment "redwood-private" with subnets: controller (priv), serving (gpu), kms-access, mgmt (bastion). Firewall rules: tight egress to KMS endpoints and Solaria monitoring stack only.
- Controller tier: 3x m6-standard-equivalent VMs (control-plane services: orchestration, scheduler, metrics aggregator). These can be lightweight CPUs (16 vCPU, 64GiB RAM) and attached to 500 GiB encrypted disk (for state, logs).
- Serving tier: a mixed GPU pool to support cost vs latency profiles: 
  - 4x GPU nodes (A) with 2x 80GB class GPUs (for heavy/low-latency workloads) -- used for pinned low-latency models.
  - 6x GPU nodes (B) with 4x 48–80GB GPUs or quantized 40GB-equivalent (for high throughput, lower priority jobs).
  - 2x cold-gpu nodes (C) with 1–2 smaller GPUs for low-cost batch runs, preemptible where allowed.
- Storage:
  - Local NVMe on GPU nodes for model KV cache and runtime temp storage (recommended: 2TB NVMe each).
  - NFS (or Ceph) for model artifacts, checkpoints and shared mounts: cluster export with encrypted at-rest storage, 50TB initial capacity, growable.
- Networking: 25Gbps node NIC minimum for GPU nodes, RDMA where available for model shards in larger configs.

Rough capacity math (back-of-envelope):
- Latency pool (4x 2x80GB nodes): each node assumed to serve ~40–90 qps for interactive flows depending on average tokens. Assume 60 qps/node -> 240 qps aggregate (meets baseline with buffer).
- Throughput pool (6x 4x48GB-equivalent): designed for batching and can absorb burst; conservative batch throughput aggregate target 600–800 qps depending on batching thresholds.
- Headroom: cold pool for overflow and model conversions.

Terraform module notes and recommended repo layout:
- Break modules into small focused blocks: network/, compute/, storage/, kms/, monitoring/, iam/. Avoid monolithic module that touches networking and compute together — customers often want to own their network.
- Input variables to highlight and make stable: cluster_name, region_alias, cidr_ranges (list), controller_instance_type, gpu_node_profiles (list of maps), kms_endpoint, storage_backend (nfs|ceph), ssh_bastion_key.
- Outputs to surface: controller_ips, serving_pool_ids, kms_ingress_cidrs, terraform_state_bucket (if remote state used).
- State handling: enforce remote state with locking (consul/s3+Dynamo style). Provide an import plan: we will import pre-existing VPCs and subnets to prevent recreation.
- Compatibility notes: current TF provider versions in our modules are pinned at aws 4.x and kubernetes 2.x; for Solaria we will publish a branch that pins to the on-prem provider equivalents (vsphere, local). Avoid using provider-level aliases that are unsupported by customer's version of vSphere.
- Migration/upgrade snippets we will include in module README: 
  - terraform state mv to move resources into new module paths.
  - example: terraform import module.network.vsphere_network.vlan_id <id>

Upgrade and rollout plan (phase 1 -> phase 2):
1) Provision baseline network and controller tier; validate access to KMS and monitoring endpoints.
2) Deploy a single small serving node and run the Redwood smoke harness: token-level latency, cold-start model load times, KV caching validation.
3) Canary deploy small fraction (5%) of traffic to latency pool; measure 99p latency and error rates for 72 hours.
4) Gradually scale to full serving pool using automated Terraform apply via CI (PRs gated by integration test suite).
5) Cutover: update DNS/routing in Solaria's edge to point to new endpoint; keep old path as fallback for 7 days.
6) Iterate performance: enable prefix caching and adjust batching thresholds in Redwood Optimize settings.

Rollback plan (short):
- If errors exceed thresholds during canary: immediate traffic shift back to previous endpoint, run drainer on new nodes, open incident.
- If persistent model regression: revert model artifact commit from artifact store and restart affected model instances with prior model.

Key terraform/ops commands for PS runbook:
- terraform init -backend-config="bucket=<state-bucket>" -reconfigure
- terraform plan -var-file=secrets.tfvars -out=plan.tfplan
- terraform apply plan.tfplan
- To drain serving node (graceful): redwoodctl node drain <node-id> --timeout 900s
- To load new model artifact: redwoodctl model deploy --artifact s3://solaria-artifacts/models/my-model:v2 --profile latency

Testing and acceptance criteria (customer-facing):
- Functional: API parity with hosted Redwood (same REST schema, streaming), key rotations through KMS succeed without service restart.
- Performance: 99th pctl latency <250ms for interactive endpoints at 200 qps sustained; 95th pctl <350ms at 600 qps burst.
- Reliability: cluster maintains 99.9% uptime during a 48-hour DR window (one node simulated down).
- Security: all egress restricted to whitelisted Solaria CIDRs and KMS endpoints; disk encryption validated.

Open questions / action items for Solaria (to resolve before finalizing playbook):
- Can Solaria expose an NTP and DNS service with consistent names for the control plane? (affects certificate TTLs)
- Confirm acceptable GPU model families and whether preemptible nodes are permitted in production.
- Provide exact KMS endpoint IPs and operator contact for firewall rules.
- Confirm retention requirements for model artifacts beyond 365 days (some teams expect longer).

Risk notes and mitigations:
- Risk: TF provider mismatch for vSphere may lead to drift or re-creation. Mitigation: perform a dry import and run diff in isolated env; avoid destructive changes in initial apply.
- Risk: model cold-start times cause transient errors. Mitigation: use warm pools and prefetch critical models during business hours.
- Risk: KMS access outage. Mitigation: caching short-lived model keys locally for a limited window and have a secondary KMS path for emergency unseal.

Appendix A — Minimal example variable block (for module consumers):

variable "cluster_name" { default = "solaria-redwood" }
variable "cidr_ranges" { type = list(string) }
variable "gpu_node_profiles" { type = list(object({ name = string, count = number, gpu_type = string, gpu_per_node = number })) }

Example tfvars snippet:
cluster_name = "solaria-redwood"
cidr_ranges = ["10.120.0.0/16"]
gpu_node_profiles = [
  { name = "latency", count = 4, gpu_type = "A100-80GB", gpu_per_node = 2 },
  { name = "throughput", count = 6, gpu_type = "A40-48GB", gpu_per_node = 4 }
]
Notes to SE/PS team:
- Bring a small perf harness (we have a canonical script in infra/tests/solaria-harness.sh) to run during the single-node smoke test.
- Prepare rollback artifacts in advance (model artifact v1 pinned in artifact store) and a playbook for node evacuation.

Next steps (short list):
- Action: Share this draft with Solaria infra owners and ask for answers to open questions (timeline: 3 business days).
- Action: Create branch in private-deploy-modules to adapt providers for vSphere and put together an import plan (owner: Diego, ETA 1 week).
- Action: Schedule 2-hour combined runbook walk-through with Solaria and PS (owner: Marcus, ETA 2 business days).

End of draft.
